trips.title: Lofoten Islands
trips.summary: A week of midnight sun, red rorbu cabins and granite peaks rising straight out of the Norwegian Sea.

trips.title: Kyoto in autumn
trips.summary: Temple gardens at peak momiji, early trains to beat the crowds and far too much matcha.

trips.title: Patagonia W-Trek
trips.summary: Five days, 80 kilometres and four seasons a day on the classic W route through Torres del Paine.

entries.title: The light that refuses to leave
paragraphs: We rolled into Reine just before midnight and the sun was still hanging above the ridge like it had forgotten its way home. The red rorbu cabins glowed against the water and nobody on the bridge was talking.
Dinner was stockfish soup from the only kitchen still open. The owner told us the cod racks would be empty in a few weeks, and that the gulls know the schedule better than anyone.
Note for next time: blackout curtains are not optional.

entries.title: Turquoise water, Arctic temperatures
paragraphs: Haukland looks like the Caribbean right up until you put a toe in. Six degrees, according to the sign, and it felt optimistic.

We walked the old road around Mannen instead of climbing it, watching the clouds pour over the summit like milk. On the far side, Uttakleiv was empty except for a family of oystercatchers who very much wanted us gone.
Best decision of the day: the thermos of hot chocolate we almost left in the car.

entries.title: Momiji, at last
paragraphs: We timed it right. Eikandō was at full colour: every maple a different shade between saffron and blood orange, reflected twice in the pond.
The pagoda on the hill is worth every step. From the top, the city fades into haze and the only sound is the temple broom scraping leaves off the stone path, a job that will never, ever be finished.
Afterwards, yudofu at a tiny place by Nanzen-ji. Tofu has no right to be this good.

entries.title: Walking with the philosophers
paragraphs: Two kilometres of canal, stone and cats. The Philosopher’s Path is supposed to be about cherry blossoms, but in late November it belongs to the maples and the locals walking their dogs.
We stopped at Hōnen-in, where the sand mounds by the gate are raked into a new pattern every season. This week: falling leaves and flowing water.
Bought a hand-dyed furoshiki from the woman who made it. She wrapped it in another furoshiki.

entries.title: Wind you can lean on
paragraphs: The catamaran across Lago Pehoé was the calmest part of the day. Once we stepped off at Paine Grande, the wind hit like a door slammed open, and it never really closed.
Gusts of 90 km/h flattened the grass and stole one of our hats somewhere over the lake. The rangers call it a mild day. We call it character building.
The refugio had hot showers, a warm stove and a view of the Cuernos turning pink at sunset. We earned every second of it.

entries.title: The towers at sunrise
paragraphs: Alarm at 3:30. Headlamps on. The last hour to the mirador is a boulder field that does not care how tired your legs are.

We made it with ten minutes to spare. When the sun hit the three granite towers they went from grey to orange to gold in under a minute, and the glacial lake below turned an impossible shade of green.
Eighty kilometres done. Patagonia, thank you for the blisters.
